title: La succession: France’s wealthiest family said to be battling over who will take over LVMH
summary:
Bernard Arnault’s children – described as ‘modern-day French royals’ – are subject of rivalry rumours over who will succeed him

They are France’s richest family, leading the world’s biggest…

blocks.text: They are France’s richest family, leading the world’s biggest luxury goods empire, dressed in matching Dior suits – a clan so powerful they have been described as modern-day French royals.

But in recent months, the family dynasty of Bernard Arnault, 77, the billionaire head of the LVMH group whose brands range from Louis Vuitton handbags to Tiffany jewellery, has become the subject of speculation about internal rivalry over which of his children could take over the company.

This week it emerged that the health-conscious Arnault, who likes to play tennis with the Swiss champion Roger Federer, can continue to lead the family holding company until he is 95, according to a new filing, pushing back any decisions on his succession.
Last year, the age cap of Arnault’s chief executive role at LVMH was raised to 85 to allow him to stay on in the position. The fashion tycoon once joked about still leading the business at 100.

blocks.caption: Bernard Arnault (centre) with his wife, Hélène, in Paris in 2021, with (from left): Frederic Arnault, Delphine Arnault, Antoine Arnault and Alexandre Arnault. Photograph: Chesnot/Getty

blocks.text: The question of which of Arnault’s five adult children could eventually lead the family company is seen as key to the French economy and the political class.
LVMH, which has more than 75 brands including fashion, perfumes and champagne, is a big employer in France.

Arnault, nicknamed the “wolf in cashmere” for his acquisitions of leading brands and whose personal wealth is estimated at more than $100bn, owns almost all of France’s business and economic press as well as the daily newspaper Le Parisien and the celebrity magazine Paris Match.
He attended Donald Trump’s second inauguration, as a personal friend, and is regularly present at official French state dinners with world leaders.

This month, Émilie Lanez published an account of what she called the emotional tensions inside the Arnault family’s unresolved succession challenge, based on what she said were hours of off-record conversations with insiders. “I was really struck by the family’s ethereal, otherworldly nature: they are like deities in a performance, and France is a spectator,” she said.

blocks.caption: Delphine Arnault, the CEO of Dior, receives an honorary doctorate in South Korea in November. Photograph: YONHAP/EPA

blocks.text: The book, Monsieur et les siens, now in discussion over a possible publication in English, traces the family’s story from Arnault’s childhood in Roubaix, in the former industrial heartland of northern France, where he took over his family’s building company before moving into property development and then luxury goods.

Lanez describes Arnault’s wife, the classical pianist Hélène Mercier-Arnault, working out on her treadmill in the early morning watching the HBO series Succession about a family business power-struggle, and then being at pains to publicly deny any rift or friction among the Arnault children.

The book depicts Arnault’s deep personal involvement in his children’s education. Schooling was so important in his own upbringing that when at age 10 he said farewell to his grandfather at his funeral, he put his glowing school report card into his grandfather’s clasped hands in his coffin.

When he had two children with his first wife, Anne Dewavrin, he devised a system to personally teach his daughter Delphine to read at a young age. At 51, she is now the chief executive of Christian Dior Couture, one of the most important roles at LVMH. Her brother Antoine, 49, has an important communications role, running the group’s image and environmental strategy.

blocks.caption: From left: Frederic Arnault, CEO of Loro Piano, Alexandre Arnault, deputy CEO of Moët Hennessy, and Antoine Arnault, head of image and sustainability at LVMH in July. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty

blocks.text: Arnault later married Mercier-Arnault and had three more sons who all work for LVMH brands. Alexandre, 34, is deputy chief executive of the drinks brand Moët Hennessy; Frédéric, 32, runs the luxury fashion brand Loro Piana; and Jean, 28, is watch director at Louis Vuitton.

When the youngest three were teenagers and preparing for higher education, Lanez writes that Arnault personally hired and interviewed tutors. The boys would come home from their day’s classes, then study with a tutor from 8pm to 11pm then go to their father’s room so he could ask them about the equations they had been tackling.

“They are likened to royals because of the power and influence they have in France,” said Lanez. “And also because they have a kind of court, courtesans and counsellors. It’s a dynasty, and the children, particularly the three youngest, have been raised to perpetuate the empire.”

Just as Arnault as a child would be shown round his father’s family building business, he regularly took his own children, and then grandchildren, on his favourite weekend activity: inspecting his luxury shops.

Arnault is aware that any family divisions can make a company vulnerable. This year, when Mercier-Arnault was promoting her latest classical music record, she did a high-profile round of media interviews in France, seeking to reassure that there were no rifts between the five children.

blocks.caption: From left: Alexandre Arnault, Bernard Arnault, Hélène Mercier-Arnault, Jean Arnault, Frédéric Arnault and Antoine Arnault attend the reopening of Tiffany’s flagship store in New York in 2023. Photograph: Cindy Ord/Getty for Tiffany & Co

blocks.text: But with the Arnaults’ vast wealth often cited as an example of the growing power of billionaires in France amid widening economic inequality, Mercier-Arnault’s comments were scrutinised.
French media reported that in an edited radio segment she had said that being homeless could be seen as a “lifestyle choice”.

Mercier-Arnault said later on a TV show that there had been a misunderstanding and she had been referring to her experience as the carer of her late sister, a violinist who was bipolar and had died by suicide, and who had begun a relationship with a person who was homeless. She told the newspaper Libération she was “deeply sorry”.

blocks.caption: Delphine Arnault with her husband, Xavier Niel, attend a state dinner near the Palace of Versailles. Photograph: Ludovic Marin/AFP/Getty

blocks.text: The cast of characters in the Arnault clan includes another high-profile and influential French billionaire, the telecoms executive Xavier Niel, who is the life-partner of Delphine Arnault. The couple have two children.
“The arrival of Xavier Niel in this family was like a theatrical scenario,” Lanez said, comparing the family saga to a novel.
Asked by the Guardian to comment on the book and speculation of tension or rivalry over the succession, LVMH declined to comment.

In July, Arnault, commenting on a series about him in Le Monde, joked about his family being likened to royals, but added that the comparison was good for sales at Dior. He said there were no divisions in the family or between his children, writing on social media that it was possible for “five strong personalities to work in the same firm without it turning into an Italian opera”.
